summary: Defines using a MIME multipart/related structure to bundle an HTML page with the images and other resources it references, and a Content-Location header that lets links point to other parts of the same bundle. It obsoletes RFC 2110.

plainLanguage.summary: An HTML page is one text file plus the images, style sheets and other files it points at. A browser fetches each of those separately from the network. This RFC lets a sender put the page and everything it points at into a single email message, so the recipient does not need network access to see it.

questions: send html page with images in email
subtitle: How to pack an HTML page and everything it references into one MIME message, and how links find their parts.

tldr.problem: An HTML page normally pulls in its images and other resources one by one from web addresses. That fails for recipients who only have email, and for pages whose resources sit on a server the recipient cannot reach.
tldr.mechanism: The page and every resource it references are bundled in one MIME multipart/related message, and a new Content-Location header labels each part with a URI so links in the page can be matched to parts of the same bundle.
tldr.outcome: A complete multi-resource HTML document travels or is archived as a single message. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2110 and drops its Content-Base header.

facts.label: type parameter value
facts.value: multipart/alternative when the start part is multipart/alternative

today: RFC 2557 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999. It obsoletes RFC 2110, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Sending a Whole Document in One Message
sections.content:
HTML (RFC 1866) defines a means of specifying multimedia documents. Such a document consists of a text/html root resource and other subsidiary resources, such as images, video clips and applets, referenced by Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) within the root resource. When a browser retrieves such a document, each component resource is individually retrieved in real time, from a location and using a protocol specified by each URI.

To transfer a complete HTML multimedia document in a single email message, two things are needed: the root resource and all the subsidiary resources it references must be aggregated into a single composite message structure, and there must be a defined way for URIs in the root to reference subsidiary resources within that structure.

RFC 2557 provides both. It defines the use of a MIME multipart/related structure to aggregate the root and the resources it references, and it specifies a MIME content header, Content-Location, that allows URIs in a multipart/related root body part to reference subsidiary resources in other body parts of the same structure.

The same conventions can be used for resources retrieved by other transfer protocols such as HTTP and FTP, and for storing complete web pages as they appeared at one moment. The RFC states that there is no requirement for a conforming implementation to handle URI-linked document representations other than those whose root is HTML.

The RFC also gives the reason it does not recommend only the Content-ID label: it should be possible to forward existing web pages by email without rewriting their source text, and rewriting has disadvantages, one of them that security checksums will probably be invalidated.
sections.plainLanguage: An HTML page is one text file plus the images, style sheets and other files it points at. A browser fetches each of those separately from the network. This RFC lets a sender put the page and everything it points at into a single email message, so the recipient does not need network access to see it.

sections.title: The Content-Location Header
sections.content:
Content-Location is the one MIME content header defined by the RFC. It can occur in any message or content heading, and its syntax is content-location = "Content-Location:" [CFWS] URI [CFWS], where the URI is restricted to the syntax for URLs as defined in RFC 1738 until IETF specifies other kinds of URIs.

A Content-Location header specifies a URI that labels the content of the body part in whose heading it is placed. Its value CAN be an absolute or a relative URI. Any URI or URL scheme may be used, but the RFC warns that use of non-standardized schemes might entail some risk that recipients cannot handle them correctly.

The URI need not refer to a resource that is globally available for retrieval. It can label a resource that only some recipients can reach, such as one inside a company-internal web space, and it can even be a fictitious URI. If the URI is absolute, or resolvable to an absolute URI, it SHOULD still be globally unique.

A single Content-Location header field is allowed in any message or content heading, in addition to a Content-ID header and, in message headings, a Message-ID. The RFC states that all of these constitute different, equally valid body part labels, and that any of them may be used to satisfy a reference to a body part. Multiple Content-Location header fields in the same message heading are not allowed.

The URI of an MHTML aggregate is not the same as the URI of its root. The root's URI retrieves only the root resource, even if it may cause a browser to separately retrieve in-line linked resources. If a Content-Location header is used in the heading of a multipart/related, that Content-Location SHOULD apply to the whole aggregate, not to its root part.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of the message gets a label, the Content-Location header, holding one web address. A link in the page is matched to a part by comparing that link with the labels of the other parts. The address does not have to be one that works on the Internet; it can name a file inside a company network or be made up.

sections.title: Encoding URIs in Header Fields
sections.content:
Some documents contain URIs with characters that are inappropriate for an RFC 822 header, either because the URI itself has an incorrect syntax according to RFC 1738, or because the URI syntax standard has been changed to allow characters not previously allowed in MIME headers. Such URIs cannot be sent directly in a message header.

When that happens, all spaces and other illegal characters in the URI must be encoded using one of the methods described in Section 4 of RFC 2047. This encoding MUST only be done in the header, not in the HTML text, and receiving clients MUST decode it in the heading before comparing URIs in body text to URIs in Content-Location headers.

The charset parameter value US-ASCII SHOULD be used if the URI contains no octets outside the 7-bit range. If such octets are present, the correct charset parameter value SHOULD be used. If this cannot be safely established, the value UNKNOWN-8BIT from RFC 1428 MUST be used. The RFC notes that the charset parameter is irrelevant for matching URIs, but that incorrect labelling must still be avoided.

Since MIME header fields have a limited length, long URIs can produce Content-Location headers that exceed it, so those headers may have to be folded. The encoding of Section 4.4.1 MUST be done before such folding, and the folding itself uses the algorithm defined in Section 3.1 of RFC 822. On receipt, folded header fields should be unfolded and then any MIME encoding removed, to retrieve the original URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A web address cannot always be written directly in a mail header, because it may contain spaces or other characters a header cannot hold. The sender must then encode those characters using the rules of MIME part 3, and the receiver must decode them before comparing. Encoding happens before a long address is folded across lines.

sections.title: Base URIs for Relative References
sections.content:
Relative URIs inside the contents of MIME body parts are resolved against a base URI, using the methods for resolving relative URIs described in RFC 1808. To determine that base URI, the first applicable method in the RFC's list applies.

  1. There is a base specification inside the MIME body part containing the relative URI. HTML provides the BASE element for this purpose.
  2. There is a Content-Location header in the immediately surrounding heading of the body part and it contains an absolute URI. This URI can serve as a base in the same way as a requested URI can serve as a base for relative URIs within a file retrieved via HTTP.
  3. If necessary, step two is repeated recursively to find a suitable Content-Location header in a surrounding multipart or message heading.
  4. If the MIME object is returned in an HTTP response, use the URI used to initiate the request.
  5. When the methods above do not yield an absolute URI, a base URL of thismessage:/ MUST be employed.

The RFC says the thismessage:/ base URL was defined for the sole purpose of resolving relative references within a multipart/related structure when no other base URI is specified. In the example in Section 9.4 of the RFC, an HTML part contains <IMG SRC="ietflogo.gif"> and a later part carries Content-Location: ietflogo.gif, so the two match once the relative reference is resolved against thismessage:/.
sections.plainLanguage: A relative link such as images/logo.gif only means something relative to a starting point. The RFC lists where to look for that starting point, and the first one that applies wins. If nothing supplies one, the starting point is thismessage:/, a made-up address that means this very message.

sections.title: Using the multipart/related Structure
sections.content:
If a message contains one or more MIME body parts containing URIs and also contains, as separate body parts, the resources those URIs refer to, then the whole set of body parts SHOULD be sent within a multipart/related structure as defined in RFC 2389.

When the start body part is an atomic object such as a text/html resource, it SHOULD be employed as the root resource. When the start body part is a multipart/alternative structure that contains at least one suitable atomic object, that body part SHOULD be the root. The RFC warns that some receiving agents treat multipart/alternative as if it were multipart/mixed.

The type parameter is mandatory in the Content-Type: multipart/related header and names the type of the start object. Its value therefore is multipart/alternative when the start part is of that type, even if the actual root resource is of type text/html. If the start object is not the first body part, its Content-ID MUST be specified as the value of a start parameter in the same header.

The RFC lists what bundling is good for: recipients who only have email but not full Internet access; recipients who for other reasons, such as firewalls or company-internal links, cannot retrieve the referenced resources over a protocol; sending a document whose content is preserved even if the resources it links to are later changed or deleted; resources that are not available for protocol-based retrieval; and speeding up access.

When a sending agent sends objects retrieved from the web, it SHOULD maintain their web URIs and not transform them, so that the receiving agent can verify message integrity codes and verify the documents against their web counterparts. Within one multipart/related structure, each body part MUST have, if assigned, a different Content-ID header value and Content-Location header field values that resolve to different URIs. Two body parts may share the same relative Content-Location value only if they resolve to different absolute URIs.

A text/html resource sent without its subsidiary resources MAY be sent by itself, without a multipart/related wrapper. Section 6 of the RFC explains why this sometimes matters: not all email recipients have full Internet connectivity, and URIs that work for a sender will not work for a recipient, for example when the URI refers to a resource inside a company-internal network.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message holds both a part that contains links and the parts those links name, the whole set should go in one multipart/related structure. The first part is the page the reader sees. Within one structure, no two parts may share a label.

sections.title: Matching Links to Body Parts
sections.content:
Section 8.2 of the RFC gives the resolution procedure for URIs in text/html body parts, in five steps.

  1. Unfold multiple line header values according to RFC 822. Do NOT translate character encodings of the kind described in RFC 1738: do not transform a%2eb/c%20d into a/b/c d.
  2. Remove all MIME encodings, such as content-transfer encoding and header encodings. Again do not translate the character encodings of the kind described in RFC 1738.
  3. Resolve all relative URIs in the HTML content and in Content-Location headers using the procedure in Section 5. The result can be an absolute URI, or an absolute URI with the base thismessage:/.
  4. For each referencing URI, compare the value after resolution with the URI derived from the Content-ID and Content-Location headers for other body parts within the same or a surrounding multipart/related structure. If the strings are identical, octet by octet, the referencing URI references that body part. This means that if one of the two URIs is a fictitious absolute URI with the base thismessage:/, the other must also be such a fictitious absolute URI.
  5. If step four fails, try to retrieve the referenced resource through ordinary Internet lookup.

Section 8.3 adds a rule for the CID scheme. When URIs employing the CID scheme are used to reference other body parts in an MHTML multipart/related structure, they MUST only be matched against Content-ID header values, and not against a Content-Location header with a CID value. The RFC gives the example: with Content-ID: <foo@bar.net> and Content-Location: CID: foo@bar.net, only the Content-ID value is matched and the Content-Location value is ignored. Content-IDs MUST be globally unique, so it is not permitted to make them unique only within a message or within a single multipart/related structure.

Section 7 of the RFC sets the limits of the scheme. It covers URIs in a resource in a nested multipart/related structure that reference body parts in the structure enclosing it. It does not cover a resource in one multipart/related structure referencing body parts in another parallel or nested structure, or in another MIME message.
sections.plainLanguage: The reader works through the parts in order. It removes the mail encoding from the link, resolves the link against the starting point, and then compares the result with the labels of the other parts, character by character. Only an exact match counts. If nothing matches, the reader may fetch the resource over the Internet as usual.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
It is possible for a message sender to misrepresent the source of a multipart/related body part by labeling it with a Content-Location URI that references another resource. Recipients should therefore only interpret Content-Location URIs as labelling a body part for the resolution of references from body parts in the same structure, and not as the source of a resource, unless this can be verified by other means.

URIs, especially file URIs, used without change in a message may inadvertently reveal information that was not intended to be revealed outside a particular security context. Senders should take care that the new header fields do not reveal information outside the security contexts to which they belong. Some resource servers hide passwords and access tickets in non-visible fields or URIs within an HTML resource, and forwarding such a resource in an email message may reveal them.

The RFC also notes that HTML documents can contain executable content directly, such as JavaScript, or reference it indirectly, and that it is exceedingly dangerous for a receiving agent to execute content received in a mail message without careful attention to restrictions on the capabilities of that content. It adds that an inline link to an object not included in the message can reveal who is reading the message, because the reader's mailer or browser will request the object over HTTP.

For caching, the RFC states that when a text/html body part in an MHTML multipart/related structure is rendered, all URIs in it that reference subsidiary resources within the same structure SHALL be satisfied by those resources and not by resources from any other local or remote source. A sender who wants the recipient always to retrieve a resource from its source MUST NOT include a labeled copy of it in the same structure. A resource received in a multipart/related structure MUST NOT be retrieved from a cache other than by a reference contained in a body part of the same structure, because failing to honour this would allow the structure to be used as a Trojan Horse to inject bogus resources into a recipient's generally accessible web cache.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can put a label on a part that claims it came from somewhere else, so a reader should treat labels only as names inside the message. A part that was received inside such a message must not be served from a shared web cache, because that would let a message insert false copies of other sites into the cache.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2110
sections.content:
RFC 2557 replaces RFC 2110, and Section 12 of the RFC lists the differences.

  • The formats described do not only apply to multipart MIME in email, but also to multipart MIME transferred through other protocols such as HTTP or FTP.
  • In order to agree with RFC 1808, Content-Location headers in multipart content headings can now be used as a base to resolve relative URIs in their component parts, but only if no base URI can be derived from the component part itself. Base URIs in Content-Location header fields in inner headings have precedence over base URIs in outer multipart headings.
  • The Content-Base header, which was present in RFC 2110, has been removed. A conservative implementor may choose to accept it in input for compatibility, but MUST never send a Content-Base header, since it is no longer part of the standard.
  • Section 4.4.1 was added, specifying how to handle the case of sending a body part whose URI does not agree with the correct URI syntax.
  • The handling of relative and absolute URIs for matching between body parts was merged into a single description, by specifying that relative URIs which cannot be resolved otherwise should be handled as if they had the URL thismessage:/.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the MHTML standard. It removed the Content-Base header, added a rule for addresses that do not fit the header syntax, and extended the formats to multipart MIME carried over HTTP or FTP as well as email.
